[[File:Kuni-no-miyatsuko of ancient Japan.jpg|thumb|300px|Map of kokuzo distribution]]
'''Kuni no miyatsuko''' (くにのみやつこ; also read ''kokuzo'' or ''kokuso'') was a type of official position in the local administrative structure of ancient Japan, based on the traditional clan-surname (ujikabane) system, who governed the provinces. The term also refers to the persons who held such positions. The [[ヤマト王権|Yamato Court]] recognized the territory of a ''kuni'' (province) as an administrative unit and designated its head as kuni no miyatsuko.

From the [[古墳時代|Kofun period]] onward, local powerful clans (gōzoku) that had long dominated the region were appointed to this role, and just as before, they continued to exercise military authority ([[国造軍|kokuzo-gun]]),<ref>They were also mobilized for foreign campaigns by order of the [[ヤマト王権|Yamato Court]].</ref> administrative authority, and judicial authority within their kuni. However, they became subordinate to the [[大和朝廷|Yamato Court]] and shifted to a position of being appointed by it.

After the [[大化の改新|Taika Reform]] and the beginning of the [[律令制|Ritsuryo system]], kokuzo lost their governing authority and became a hereditary honorary title, primarily responsible for overseeing ceremonies and rituals ('''Ritsuryo kokuzo''').

Under the Ritsuryo system, the former local clans occupied the ranks of local officials called [[郡司|gunji]], and the traditional ujikabane system continued to support the Ritsuryo system in the provinces. The clans also continued to maintain armed forces and breed horses. In the early [[平安時代|Heian period]], their decline accelerated and they were replaced by a new class of provincial elite.

== Overview ==
The kuni no miyatsuko was the head of a ''kuni'', one of the administrative units of the [[ヤマト王権|Yamato Court]]. Since these kuni predated the establishment of the [[令制国|Ritsuryo provincial system]], their boundaries are not clearly defined. It is thought that the territory controlled by regional powerful clans was treated as a kuni. Influential clans were either dispatched by the court or submitted to it and were appointed as kokuzo, with many receiving [[カバネ|kabane]] (clan surnames) such as [[臣|omi]], [[連|muraji]], [[キミ (カバネ)|kimi]] (kō), and [[直 (姓)|atai]] (ōnaotai) in the court of [[允恭天皇|Emperor Ingyō]]. Unlike the [[県主|agata-nushi]], who were directly under Yamato Court control, kokuzo were granted broad autonomy including military and judicial authority.

The earliest establishment of kokuzo appears in records from the court of [[神武天皇|Emperor Jinmu]], and systematic establishment began in earnest during the reign of [[崇神天皇|Emperor Sujin]], along routes of the [[四道将軍|Four Generals' expeditions]]. In the court of [[景行天皇|Emperor Keikō]], chiefs were placed throughout the land in coordination with the emperor's western expeditions and [[倭建命|Yamato Takeru]]'s eastern expeditions, and in the subsequent court of [[成務天皇|Emperor Seimu]], kokuzo were established in rapid succession. Details of these appointments appear in the [[国造本紀|Kokuzo Hongi]], and records of the establishment of the kuni-agata system by Emperor Seimu also appear in the [[記紀|Kiki]]. Some kokuzo were established later in the court of [[応神天皇|Emperor Ōjin]], and others were divided and redistributed during the court of [[仁徳天皇|Emperor Nintoku]].

The kabane given to kokuzo by the Ōkimi (Great King) varied:
# Atai-kabane kokuzo in [[畿内#日本の畿内|Kinai]] and surrounding provinces
# Omi-kabane kokuzo in [[吉備国|Kibi]] and [[出雲国|Izumo]]
# Ōnaotai-kabane kokuzo in parts of [[山陽道]] and [[南海道]]
# Tomomiyatsuko-kabane kokuzo, named for groups under the ''namishiro no tomonozukuri'' system, in the [[東海道]] and [[東山道]] regions
# Kimi-kabane kokuzo in the eastern [[毛野]] (Keno) region and the western [[筑紫国|Tsukushi]], [[豊国|Toyo]], and [[肥国|Hi]] regions

This variety shows that the organization was not uniform.

Kokuzo presided over the worship of ancestral deities (ujigami) of their respective kokuzo clans, and also managed [[部民|be-no-tami]] (clan workers) and [[屯倉|miyake]] (royal granaries). Daughters and sons of kokuzo clans served at court as [[舎人|toneri]] (attendants) and [[釆女|uneme]] (palace women), and some, such as the [[紀国造|Ki no Kokuzo]] and [[上毛野国造|Kamitsukeno no Kokuzo]], were involved in diplomacy. There were also kokuzo, such as the [[筑紫国造|Tsukushi no Kokuzo]], who brought northern Kyushu under their control and rebelled against the Yamato Court, and some, like the [[闘鶏国造|Tōchi Kokuzo]], were dissolved.

Below the kokuzo were [[古代日本の地方官制#県（アガタ）|agata]] (sub-districts), and some scholars hold that there was a fairly developed kuni-agata system. However, many aspects of local governance before the Ritsuryo system remain unclear, including the actual state of the kokuzo system and relationships with medium and small clans.

Kokuzo endured for a long time through the Kofun period, but from the late [[6世紀|6th century]] (reign of [[推古天皇|Empress Suiko]]) to the mid-[[7世紀|7th century]] (reign of [[孝徳天皇|Emperor Kōtoku]]), kokuzo throughout the land were changed to [[評督|hyō-toku]] (district overseers), and after the Taika Reform, when the [[大宝令|Taihō Code]] came into effect, hyō were replaced by gun (counties), with some kokuzo also holding concurrent positions as [[郡領|gunryō]] (county officials).

The [[国造本紀|Kokuzo Hongi]] (Volume 10 of the [[先代旧事本紀|Sendai Kuji Hongi]]), believed to have been compiled in the [[9世紀|9th century]], contains records of 135 kokuzo throughout the country, including their establishment periods and those who were appointed.

== Ritsuryo Kokuzo ==
After the Taika Reform, the kuni governed by kokuzo were reorganized, consolidated, or divided and replaced by the Ritsuryo provincial system; nevertheless, kokuzo continued to exist under the Ritsuryo framework. These are called '''Ritsuryo Kokuzo'''. They became a hereditary honorary title primarily overseeing rituals, concurrently held by gunji — descendants of the former kokuzo. Kokuzo also received allocated rice fields known as kokuzo-den. Subsequently, from the latter half of the [[8世紀|8th century]] onward, kokuzo gradually disappeared. In modern scholarship, to distinguish kokuzo under the ujikabane system from Ritsuryo Kokuzo, a convention exists: for example, the former is written as ''Kazusa no Kuni no Miyatsuko'' (上総国造) and the latter as ''Kazusa no Kuni no Kokuzo'' (上総国国造).

=== List of Non-Existent Kokuzo ===
The following kokuzo appear in shrine traditions and texts such as Volume 28 of the ''Suwa Shiryō'' (containing the "Suwa Shimosha Ōhōri Takei-nohafuri Lineage Chart Abbreviated"), and the apocryphal works ''[[先代旧事本紀大成経|Sendai Kuji Hongi Taiseikyo]]'', ''[[科野国造|Aso-ke Ryakukeizu]]'', ''Shūho Suwa-shi Keizu Seien'', and ''Shokeifu''; however, since their credibility is low and they cannot be corroborated in other historical sources, they are considered to have not actually existed.

== Kokuzo that Survived After the Taika Reform ==
=== Main New Kokuzo ===
* [[出雲国造|Izumo no Kuni Kokuzo]] (Kizuki Kokuzo)
*: As the supreme Shinto priest of [[出雲大社|Izumo Taisha]], they were revered almost like a living deity (''arahitogami''). During the [[南北朝時代 (日本)|Northern and Southern Courts period]], they split into the Senke and Kitajima branches, but they continue today as shrine families of Izumo Taisha.
* [[紀伊国造|Ki no Kuni Kokuzo]]
*: Shrine family of [[日前神宮・国懸神宮]]. The family line lapsed in the early [[平安時代|Heian period]] and mid-[[江戸時代|Edo period]], but was maintained through maternal succession. Currently uses the Fujiwara surname.

==== Kokuzo Clans that Transmitted Their Lineage as Warrior Families ====
* [[那須国造|Nasu Kokuzo]] — Claims to be of Fujiwara Nagaie lineage, but some assert that they intermarried with the kokuzo family to become the later Nasu clan.

==== Kokuzo Clans that Transmitted Their Lineage as Shrine Families ====
* [[阿尺国造|Asaka Kokuzo]] (Asaka Kokuzo)
*: The Ando family, shrine family of [[安積国造神社|Asaka Kokuzo Shrine]] in Kōriyama City, Fukushima Prefecture. They claim descent from the Asaka Kokuzo clan and use the Asaka surname.
* [[石背国造|Iwase Kokuzo]]
* [[无邪志国造|Musashi Kokuzo]]
* [[伊豆国造|Izu Kokuzo]]
* [[尾張国造|Owari Kokuzo]]
*: Head family of [[熱田神宮|Atsuta Jingū]]
* [[出雲国造|Izumo Kokuzo]] (Kizuki Kokuzo)
* [[熊野国造|Kumano Kokuzo]]
*: Shrine family of Kumano Taisha
* [[科野国造|Shinano Kokuzo]]
*: The [[金刺氏|Kanasashi clan]], head priests (''Ōhōri'') of [[諏訪大社|Suwa Taisha]] (Lower Shrine). Later defeated in conflict with the Suwa clan and extinguished, with the collateral [[武居氏|Takei clan]] taking over.
* [[斐陀国造|Hida Kokuzo]]
* [[角鹿国造|Tsunuga Kokuzo]]
* [[穂国造|Ho Kokuzo]]
*: Shrine family of [[砥鹿神社|Tonoshiro Shrine]]
* [[但島国造|Tajima Kokuzo]]
* [[丹波国造|Tanba Kokuzo]]
*: The [[海部氏|Amabe family]], shrine family of [[籠神社|Kono Shrine]] in Miyazu City, Kyoto Prefecture. The current high priest claims to be the 82nd Tanba Kokuzo. The [[海部氏系図|Amabe clan genealogy]] is a National Treasure.
* [[凡河内国造|Ōshikouchi Kokuzo]]
* [[賀陽国造|Kaya Kokuzo]]
* [[三野国造|Mino Kokuzo]]
* [[億岐国造|Oki Kokuzo]]
* [[宇佐国造|Usa Kokuzo]]
*: Shrine family of [[宇佐神宮|Usa Jingū]]
* [[阿蘇国造|Aso Kokuzo]]
*: The [[阿蘇氏|Uji clan]], later renamed Aso clan. As warlords during the [[戦国時代 (日本)|Sengoku period]], they were destroyed in the [[阿蘇合戦|Aso War]], but [[加藤清正|Kato Kiyomasa]] restored [[阿蘇惟種|Aso Koretane]]'s orphan [[阿蘇惟善|Koretomo]] as head priest. They continue to exist as the head priest family to this day.
* [[日向国造|Hyūga Kokuzo]]
* [[因幡国造|Inaba Kokuzo]]
*: The [[伊福部氏|Ifukube clan]], who served as ''kannagi'' (ritual officiants) at [[宇倍神社|Ube Shrine]] and claimed the title Inaba Kokuzo, were actually a branch lineage that split off from the [[因幡氏|Inaba clan]] (Inaba Kokuzo clan), the true kokuzo.
